transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten so strange lately, especially with my eating. It's been going on for months now, this whole ordeal. It's like my stomach and my brain just aren't talking to each other anymore, if that makes any sense. Some days, I wake up and the very thought of food is just... well, it's exhausting, honestly. I'll just sit at the kitchen table, staring out the window, and all I can manage to get down is a piece of dry toast and a cup of black coffee. And even that feels like a chore, like I'm forcing myself to chew and swallow when I'd rather just sit there. But then, and this is the really bizarre part, other days it's the exact opposite. I'll be at the grocery store, just trying to get a few necessities, you know, maybe some milk or eggs, and suddenly I find myself standing in the bakery aisle. I don't even know how I get there sometimes. And I'll just start putting things in my cart—donuts, those little frosted cookies, maybe a whole cake—and I buy them, and I eat them, but I don't even really enjoy them. It's not like a treat or a craving, it's just this... compulsion, I guess. I'll sit on the couch eating a pastry, and it just tastes like ash in my mouth, but I can't stop. It's all just so turned around, and I don't know what to do about it anymore. It's really starting to bother me, this back and forth, up and down with food. It's just not like me at all.
Do you ever worry about gaining weight when you're eating or after you've eaten?

Weight? You know, it's funny you ask that, because my sister—she's always on some new diet, always counting points or whatever it is they do now—she asked me the exact same thing last week when I was trying to explain the whole bakery aisle situation to her. But no, I don't... I don't really think about the weight at all. 

It's not like when I was in my twenties or thirties and I'd worry about fitting into a certain pair of jeans, or, you know, getting ready for summer and worrying about how I looked in a swimsuit. Back then, sure, I'd eat a piece of cake and think, oh, I'm going to have to walk an extra mile tomorrow. But now? It's just... the weight doesn't even cross my mind. When I'm sitting there with those frosted cookies, it's not about indulgence, so there's no guilt about calories or getting fat or anything like that. It's more like I'm just a machine going through the motions. 

I could gain ten pounds or lose ten pounds and I honestly don't think I'd even care right now. It's just so disconnected from how I look. I mean, I don't even really look in the mirror much these days anyway, maybe just a quick glance to brush my hair in the morning so I don't look a total fright, but the number on the scale? It just feels so completely unimportant compared to how strange everything else feels. So, no, the weight isn't what bothers me about all this. It's just the... the doing it, you know? The not being able to stop even when the food tastes like absolutely nothing.
Do you fear gaining weight when you're not eating or when you're restricting your food intake?

No, no, not then either. It’s really exactly the same as when I’m overeating. When I have those days where I’m just... restricting, I guess you could call it, or just not eating because I can’t bring myself to do it, weight is the furthest thing from my mind. 

Like I was saying about the dry toast, I’m not sitting there thinking, 'Oh, good, I’m saving calories today.' It’s nothing like that. I know people do that—my neighbor, Susan, she does that intermittent fasting thing where she won't touch a crumb until noon just so she can drop a dress size for her daughter's wedding. But for me? It has absolutely nothing to do with dress sizes or getting fat. The desire is just... it's just completely gone. I could look down and see I’ve shrunk to skin and bones and I don't think it would even register as a good thing or a bad thing. It’s just this heavy emptiness. 

So when I’m sitting there, ignoring food, it’s not out of fear of the scale. The scale is just a piece of plastic on the bathroom floor collecting dust. I actually think I kicked it under the sink a few weeks ago just so I wouldn't have to sweep around it, not because I'm afraid of what it says, but just because it's another useless thing taking up space, you know? So, no, whether I’m eating a whole cake or just staring blankly at a piece of bread, gaining weight just doesn't factor into it at all. It’s really just about trying to get through the day without feeling so completely overwhelmed by the mechanics of it all.
Do you feel guilty after you've eaten, especially on those days when you're consuming a lot of food?

Guilty? You know, that's a really interesting question, doctor, because I've spent a lot of time trying to figure out exactly what it is I *do* feel after one of those grocery store episodes. And guilt... no, guilt isn't the right word at all. 

When I think of guilt, I think of, oh, I don't know, forgetting my mother's birthday, which I actually did back in 1998, and I felt just awful about it for months. Or maybe snapping at the mailman because he bent a magazine, something like that. But with the food? It's not guilt. It's more like... well, it's just this profound sense of confusion and maybe a little bit of disgust, but not at myself, just at the whole situation. 

Like last Tuesday, I had bought this enormous box of those little powdered sugar donuts. The ones that come in the crinkly bag inside the box? And I sat on the sofa, watching some daytime talk show—I don't even remember which one, maybe it was a rerun of something—and I just ate the whole box. And when I was done, I looked at the empty bag, and my fingers were all coated in white powder, and I just sat there thinking, 'Why did I do that?' I wasn't thinking, 'Oh, you bad person, you shouldn't have eaten that.' It was more like I was a spectator watching someone else do it. 

I actually went to the sink to wash the sugar off my hands, and the water was running over my fingers, and I just stared at it going down the drain for what felt like twenty minutes. Just watching the white powder dissolve and swirl away. And I felt... nothing. No remorse, no 'I promise I'll do better tomorrow.' Just this heavy, blank feeling, like someone had unplugged me from the wall. My sister, she feels guilty if she eats half a piece of garlic bread at a restaurant, she'll talk about it all the way home in the car, 'Oh, I shouldn't have done that, the carbs, the butter.' But for me, the donuts, the cake... it's just fuel that I didn't want and didn't enjoy, put into a machine that's barely running anyway. So no, doctor, no guilt. Just... just a lot of empty wrappers and wondering what on earth is happening to me.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you've started on those days when you're consuming a lot of food?

Unable to stop... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know what you mean, like people who just lose control and eat until they're sick. I saw a documentary about that once, years ago, on PBS I think, where this poor woman just couldn't physically stop herself from emptying her entire pantry. But for me? No, it’s not like that at all. 

It’s more like... I just don't care enough to stop right away, but I definitely can stop whenever I want to. Like last Thursday. I had bought this family-sized frozen lasagna—the one with the meat sauce, not the four-cheese one, because the cheese one always seems so greasy—and I heated the whole thing up. It takes almost an hour in the oven, which is a long time to just sit and wait when you're just staring at the kitchen clock, but anyway, I took it out and sat down with the pan. I ate maybe half of it. Just forkful after forkful, not really tasting the tomatoes or the pasta at all. 

But it wasn't because I couldn't stop. Actually, right in the middle of a bite, I just... stopped. I put the fork down on the counter. The phone started ringing in the hallway—it was probably a telemarketer, they always call around dinnertime, don't they, always asking for donations or trying to sell duct cleaning—and I didn't even go to answer it, but the sound of the ringing just sort of broke whatever dull routine I was in. I looked at the lasagna and just pushed the pan away. 

So I definitely can stop. I don't have that frantic feeling of needing to finish every last bite or scraping the bottom of the dish. I ended up putting some aluminum foil over the rest of the pan and sticking it in the fridge, and it just sat there taking up space on the middle shelf until garbage day on Tuesday. I had to scrape it all into the trash bag, which was a terrible mess because the sauce had completely congealed to the sides of the foil pan. But the point I'm trying to make is, I'm in control of my hands. I'm in control of the fork. It's just that my brain is sort of switched off while I'm doing the eating. But if I decide to stop, or if I just get tired of the physical act of chewing, which actually happens quite a bit lately, my jaw just gets tired... I just stop. It's not some unstoppable urge, doctor, it's just a really long, drawn-out blank space.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past few months?

Lost weight? Well, like I mentioned before with the scale being kicked under the bathroom sink, I couldn't give you a precise number. I really couldn't. But honestly, the whole reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see someone is because my eating has just gotten all turned around for months now. It's completely upside down. 

I mean, it's just this constant back and forth, and it doesn't make any sense to me. Some days, I'll just sit there at the kitchen table for hours and pick at a piece of dry toast and maybe have a few sips of coffee. I'll make a whole pot of it in the morning, just out of habit, you know, the regular drip kind in the big glass carafe, and it'll just sit there getting cold and bitter on the burner because I have absolutely zero interest in it. I'll just pick and pick at the edges of the bread until it's just crumbs on the plate. 

But then, on the flip side, other days I'll drive to the grocery store and I'll find myself just standing there in the middle of the bakery aisle. I'll stand there for I don't know how long under those bright fluorescent lights, just staring at the shelves, buying all sorts of sweets that I don't even really enjoy. I'll put a whole cherry pie or those little plastic tubs of frosted sugar cookies into my cart, and I don't even have a sweet tooth! I never really have. My ex-husband was the one who always wanted dessert after dinner, not me. But there I am, buying them anyway, just filling the cart with things I don't even want to taste. 

So with my eating being so erratic like that, swinging wildly from practically nothing to a whole bakery's worth of sugar, I honestly don't know what my weight is doing. My clothes feel a little different depending on the day, I suppose, but the whole thing is just so turned around that I couldn't tell you if I'm actually losing or gaining at this point.
Have you noticed your clothes fitting looser over the past few months?

Well, like I was just mentioning about my clothes feeling a little different depending on the day... it's really hard to say if they are strictly *looser*, just because of how completely unpredictable everything is. I mean, I have this one pair of navy blue slacks, the kind with the little bit of elastic in the back of the waistband? I bought them at JCPenney a few years ago because they're just so comfortable for running errands, they don't pinch when you sit down in the car. And some weeks, I pull them on and they do feel a bit baggy in the thighs, or maybe they slide down a little when I'm walking down the driveway to get the mail. 

But then other weeks, they feel perfectly snug again. And it all just goes right back to what I was just telling you. I mean, the whole reason I finally came in to see someone is because my eating has gotten all turned around for months now. It's just a complete mess. Because, you know, some days I'll just sit there and pick at a piece of toast and a cup of coffee, just breaking the crust into little pieces on the napkin and not even swallowing half of it. But then other days, I'm right back to standing in the middle of the bakery aisle, just staring at the shelves and buying sweets I don't even really enjoy, like those frosted cookies or the pies. 

So my body just doesn't know what to do with all that back and forth. One week I'm practically running on toast crumbs and cold coffee, and the next I'm eating a whole bakery's worth of sugar. So the clothes... they just sort of follow along with whatever my stomach is doing that week, I suppose. It's never just one direction, looser or tighter, it's just this constant, exhausting seesaw.
Are there any activities or things you used to enjoy that you've stopped doing because of your eating habits?

Because of my eating habits? Oh, no, I wouldn't say it's because of the eating. It's not like I'm staying home just to sit at the kitchen table and pick at my food instead of going out. It's... well, it's something else entirely. I have stopped doing things, yes, practically everything, but it's not because I'm busy eating. It's just because I don't have the... the spark for it anymore. 

I used to be so involved, doctor. I used to get so excited about my quilting squares. I had this whole setup in the spare bedroom, and I'd spend hours cutting out these intricate little pieces. I was working on a log cabin design, picking out all these beautiful contrasting fabrics, making sure the light and dark sides balanced just perfectly. It takes a lot of concentration, making sure your quarter-inch seams are exact, otherwise the whole block gets wonky when you try to piece it together. And bowling night, too! I used to go every single Wednesday with a group of ladies from my neighborhood. I even had my own shoes so I didn't have to rent those awful, stiff ones they spray with whatever that chemical is, and my own ball, a really pretty swirling purple one. 

And I was always the one planning the potlucks. I really loved doing that. I'd get on the phone and coordinate everything so we wouldn't end up with five green bean casseroles and no desserts, you know how that goes if someone isn't keeping track of the list. But now... I just don't know what happened. Now I look at my quilting supplies, all those expensive fabrics just sitting there gathering dust in their plastic bins, or I look at the church calendar hanging by the fridge, and I just can't make myself care the way I used to. 

It's completely gone. The excitement, I mean. It's not that my stomach is dictating my schedule, it's just that my brain looks at all those things I used to love and just feels incredibly blank. It feels like way too much effort to even pretend to care about a potluck or a bowling score. I just stare at the calendar and feel absolutely nothing.
Have you noticed any change in your weight over the past few months?

Well, doctor, I... I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here with the weight. Like I was trying to say just a few minutes ago, I really don't have a clue what the actual number on the scale is doing. The entire reason I finally made this appointment and came in here to see you is because my eating has just gotten all turned around for months now. It's completely upside down, and it has been for a long time. 

I mean, I know I already mentioned how some days I'll just sit there at the table and pick at a piece of dry toast and that cold cup of coffee, just breaking the crusts apart and not even swallowing half of it. And then, just as suddenly, other days I'm right back to standing in the middle of the bakery aisle at the grocery store, just filling my cart with cherry pies and those plastic tubs of frosted cookies that I don't even really enjoy. I don't even have a sweet tooth, but there I am anyway, buying all those sweets! 

So with my eating habits swinging back and forth like a pendulum between nothing at all and a mountain of sugar, I just can't tell you if my weight is going up, down, or sideways. I really haven't noticed a specific change in the weight itself, just that the whole routine of how I eat is a big, unpredictable mess.
Do you think your eating habits are related to a fear of gaining weight?

Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, no, no. It's nothing like that at all. Gaining weight? I mean, at my age, you sort of expect the numbers on the scale to creep up a little bit here and there, especially after menopause, which I went through a few years back and that was a whole ordeal in itself with the hot flashes and the night sweats... but no, I'm not afraid of gaining weight. That's not what's driving this whole mess with the food. 

It's not like I'm looking in the mirror and worrying about my waistline or trying to fit into some dress from twenty years ago. I'm not standing in the bakery aisle thinking, "Oh, I shouldn't buy this cherry pie because it'll go straight to my hips." I don't even care about my hips anymore! Like I was saying, half the time I don't even *want* the pie, I just buy it. And when I'm just picking at that piece of toast, it's not because I'm counting calories or trying to diet. I've never really been a dieter, honestly. I tried Weight Watchers once back in the nineties with my sister-in-law, Susan, but all that point-counting just gave me a headache, and I quit after three weeks. 

So no, it's not a fear of getting heavier. It's just... the appetite itself is completely broken. It's like the mechanism in my brain that tells me when I'm hungry or what I want to eat has just short-circuited entirely. Sometimes the thought of chewing and swallowing is just too exhausting, and other times I'm just eating without even tasting it. But it has absolutely nothing to do with being afraid of putting on a few pounds. I couldn't care less about that right now, to be perfectly honest with you.
Have you stopped enjoying or participating in activities you previously found pleasurable due to how you've been feeling lately?

Well, doctor, I... I feel like we just talked about this, didn't we? Just a few minutes ago? But yes, absolutely, it's exactly like I was saying before. It's not the food keeping me away from things, it's just... this heavy, blank feeling. 

I mean, I was telling you about my quilting, right? The log cabin design? I had all those little squares cut out, all those beautiful fabrics, and I used to just get so excited to sit in the spare room and piece them together. I'd spend hours in there, making sure every seam was just right. And the bowling on Wednesday nights with the ladies, and the church potlucks... I was the one who organized them! I loved getting on the phone and making sure everyone brought something different. I was always the one making sure things ran smoothly. 

But lately... lately it's just... I look at those plastic bins full of fabric, or I see the church calendar hanging there on the refrigerator door, and it's like I'm looking at someone else's life. I just stare at it and I can't make myself care. The excitement is just completely gone. I don't want to go to bowling, I don't want to call anyone about a casserole, I don't even want to look at my sewing machine. It's just too much effort to even pretend to be interested anymore. So yes, I've stopped doing all of it. All of it just feels so pointless now.
Have you noticed that you've lost a substantial amount of weight recently?

Doctor, I... I feel like we keep circling back to this exact same thing. Didn't we just go over this? I mean, I know I talk a lot, my late husband always used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey, bless his heart, but I really feel like I've explained this already. 

Like I was trying to tell you before, the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment—which wasn't easy, let me tell you, getting myself out of the house these days is a chore and a half—was because my eating has just gotten all turned around. It's been going on for months now. Months! 

And I just don't know what the scale says because, well, it's not a straightforward thing where I just stopped eating or started eating too much. It's all over the place! Like I mentioned, some mornings I'll just sit there at the kitchen table, staring out the window at the neighbor's yard—they never mow their lawn, by the way, it's a disgrace—and I'll just pick and pick at a piece of dry toast and a cold cup of coffee. Just pulling it apart into little crumbs and not even swallowing half of it. 

But then, out of nowhere, other days I'll find myself standing right smack in the middle of the bakery aisle at the Piggly Wiggly, just loading up my cart with cherry pies and those awful plastic tubs of frosted sugar cookies. And the thing is, I don't even really enjoy them! I don't! I've never been one for overly sweet things, I always preferred a savory snack, maybe some cheese and crackers, but there I am, buying all these sweets anyway. 

So with my eating habits swinging back and forth like that, from basically nothing to a whole cart of bakery items, I just couldn't tell you if I've lost a substantial amount of weight. I haven't noticed my clothes falling off me or anything. It's just the eating itself that's completely upside down.
Have you experienced any significant weight loss recently?

Doctor, are you... are you reading off a checklist there? Because I really do feel like I might be losing my mind, or maybe my hearing is going, but I swear on my mother's grave you just asked me that exact same question. Like, literally just a minute ago! Is there something wrong with your notepad? 

I really don't mean to be short with you, I know you doctors have a lot on your plates and you see dozens of people a day, probably all with their own set of problems, but like I was just saying... I came in because my eating has gotten all turned around. It's been going on for months now. Months and months! And it's not a simple thing where I can just step on the bathroom scale and say, "Oh, look, I've lost ten pounds," because my habits are completely out of whack. 

It's exactly like I just explained. Some days I just sit there in the kitchen and pick at a piece of dry toast and a cold cup of coffee. Just tearing the crust off, leaving crumbs everywhere on my nice placemats, not even swallowing half of it. And then, out of the blue, other days I'll be standing right there in the bakery aisle at the grocery store, buying all these sweets and pies and frosted cookies that I don't even really enjoy! I don't even have a sweet tooth! I've always been more of a salty snack person, like pretzels or some nice mixed nuts. But there I am, putting it all in the cart anyway. 

So between eating like a bird on Tuesday and buying out the Piggly Wiggly bakery on Thursday, I have absolutely no idea what my weight is doing. I haven't noticed any significant loss because my body doesn't know whether it's coming or going, and honestly, neither do I. I just know the whole routine is completely upside down right now.
Do you think your lack of interest in activities like quilting and bowling is directly related to your eating habits or is it something separate that you're experiencing?

Oh, doctor, no, I don't think it's the food at all. Like I was saying just a little bit ago—and I know I'm repeating myself, but you did ask—it feels completely separate. The eating thing is its own big mess with the bakery aisle and the dry toast, but this... this just not caring about anything? That's something else entirely. It's like a heavy, wet blanket has just been thrown over my whole life. 

I mean, I really used to get so incredibly excited about my quilting squares. I had this whole system, you know? Sorting them all by color and pattern—the blues over here, the calicos there, the little floral prints I got on sale at JoAnn Fabrics all neatly stacked up. And the bowling night with the girls, and planning those church potlucks... I practically lived for that! I was the one making the calls, organizing the sign-up sheets, making sure Mildred didn't bring her ambrosia salad again because nobody really eats it anyway. 

But now... it really has absolutely nothing to do with whether I ate a whole box of cookies or just a crumb of toast that day. I just look at my sewing supplies sitting in those plastic bins in the spare room, or I stare at the church calendar hanging right there on the fridge under the little magnet shaped like a teapot, and I just... I can't make myself care the way I used to. The spark is just entirely gone. It takes so much energy just to look at them. So, no, it's totally separate from the eating. It's just this awful, blank feeling that won't go away, no matter what my stomach is doing.
Do you feel sad or depressed most of the time?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. It's... it's hard to explain, but yes. Most days, actually. It's like I was just saying about the heavy, wet blanket, but it's more than just not caring about my quilting or the potlucks. It's this... this actual feeling. 

Most days I wake up and before I even get my feet out from under the covers, I can feel it. It's this heavy, sad feeling just sitting right on my chest, pressing down on me. And I'll drag myself out of bed, put on my fuzzy slippers—the pink ones my sister got me for Christmas three years ago, they're getting a bit worn out on the heels but they're still warm—and I'll go into the kitchen. 

Now, my kitchen is usually my favorite room in the house. I had it painted this lovely, cheerful yellow color back in 2018, like a soft buttercup yellow, because I always liked a bright room in the morning. And I'll get the coffee going, listening to the pot gurgle and smell the beans roasting, and normally that would just perk me right up. But lately... even standing right there in my bright yellow kitchen with the coffee going, I just feel like all the warmth has gone out of everything. 

It doesn't matter if the sun is shining right through the window over the sink, hitting the little crystal suncatcher I hung up there. It just feels cold and sad inside me. It just lingers there, this awful sadness, following me from the kitchen to the living room and back again, all day long. So, yes, doctor, I do feel sad most of the time. It just doesn't seem to lift, no matter what I do or what room I'm in.
Are there people in your life who have noticed a change in your eating habits or overall behavior?

Well, yes, they absolutely have. And it's not even just about the bakery items or the toast, though my sister did make a comment about my kitchen looking a bit chaotic lately. But it's more about my whole... well, just the way I'm functioning, I suppose. It's actually gotten a little embarrassing, to be perfectly honest with you.

Just last week, I was at the grocery store—the Piggly Wiggly down on 4th Street, you know, the one with the good produce section, not that cramped one over by the highway—and I was just trying to get through the canned goods aisle. And my neighbor, Sarah, she came right up to me and she actually asked if my hip was bothering me! Now, I did have a little bursitis in that left hip back in 2019 from standing too long at a bake sale, but that cleared right up years ago. But she asked because she said I was just... moving so incredibly slow through the grocery store. Shuffling, almost. Like I was walking through thick mud or molasses just to get a can of green beans. 

And it's not just my walking, either. It's at my meetings, too. We had our monthly planning meeting for the ladies' auxiliary—the one where we usually sort out the potlucks, which, like I was telling you, I just don't have the spark for anymore—but I still went because I felt obligated. And Mildred asked me the absolute simplest question. I think she just asked if we should use the cheap paper plates or the nice plastic ones for the spring luncheon. A simple, everyday question! But I just... I just sat there. I heard her perfectly fine, but it was like the words had to travel through a long tunnel to get into my brain, and then my answer had to gather up the energy to travel all the way back out. It took me forever to answer her. Just to say the word paper. Everyone was just staring at me, waiting for me to speak. 

So, yes, people are definitely noticing. They see me taking forever to answer a simple question, or moving like a snail past the checkout counters, and they just don't know what to make of it. And honestly, neither do I.
Do you think your disinterest in activities such as quilting and bowling is directly caused by your current eating habits?

Well, doctor, I know we just touched on this a few minutes ago, but I really don't think it's the eating at all. It's completely separate. Like I was saying, it's just this... this awful, heavy feeling that has nothing to do with food. 

I mean, I really used to get so incredibly excited about my quilting squares. I had that whole system, sorting them all by color and pattern—the blues, the calicos, those little floral prints from JoAnn Fabrics. And the bowling night with the girls, and planning those church potlucks... I practically lived for that! I was the one making the calls and organizing everything. 

But now... I just look at my sewing supplies sitting in those plastic bins in the spare room, or I stare at the church calendar hanging on the fridge, and I just... I can't make myself care the way I used to. The spark is entirely gone. It takes so much energy just to look at them. So, no, it really has absolutely nothing to do with whether I'm eating too much or too little. It's just this awful, blank feeling where my interests used to be.
Do you think your lack of interest in things like quilting and bowling might be related to your feelings of sadness?

Well, yes, I suppose they are tied together, aren't they? It's all part of that same heavy blanket I was telling you about. It's just... it's so strange, doctor, because I really, truly used to get so excited about all of it. I mean, my quilting squares! I had this whole beautiful system going in the spare bedroom. I had these clear plastic bins—the good ones with the latching lids so the dust wouldn't get in—and I had everything sorted. The blues over here, the calicos in the middle, and all those little floral prints I'd find on sale at JoAnn Fabrics over by the window. I could spend hours in there, just matching up colors and thinking about the patterns. 

And then there was bowling night with the girls every Thursday. We had our own shirts and everything! And planning the church potlucks... oh, I practically lived for that. I was always the one on the telephone, making sure we didn't end up with five potato salads and no desserts. I loved organizing it all. 

But now... it's like that sadness just drains the color out of everything. I'll walk past the spare room and look at those bins of quilting supplies, or I'll be in the kitchen and stare at the church calendar I have pinned to the fridge with a little magnetic apple, and I just... I can't make myself care. Not even a little bit. I look at the things I used to love, the things that used to fill up my days, and I just feel that same awful, blank, sad feeling. The spark is just entirely gone. It's like I'm looking at someone else's life, and I just don't have the energy to step back into it. So, yes, I think the sadness and the not caring... they're absolutely holding hands in all of this.
Are there any problems in your daily life or relationships that you think might be related to your eating habits?

Well, honestly, like I was saying before, I don't think it's the eating habits causing the problems, but there are definitely problems. It's that same heavy, awful feeling that's getting in the way of everything. 

I mean, I still manage to get through the absolute basics for my Aunt Martha. I make sure she has her tea in the morning, and I lay out her pills—the little blue ones and the big white one she takes for her blood pressure—because if I don't do it, she'll just forget, bless her heart. But beyond that... it's just all falling apart. 

I've completely missed the last three church planning calls. I didn't even pick up the phone when it rang, I just sat in the armchair and watched the caller ID flash Mildred's name over and over. And the county fair is coming up in just two months, and I usually have at least three quilting projects ready to enter by now. I've won blue ribbons four years running, you know! But I've just put it all off. The fabric is just sitting there in those bins, gathering dust. 

And it's not just the fun things, either. It's the day-to-day things. I've had to ask the neighbors, the Millers next door—they're lovely people, they have that beautiful golden retriever—to help out with things I used to do without a second thought. Like taking the trash cans down to the curb, or picking up Aunt Martha's prescriptions from the pharmacy. I used to handle all of that so easily.
